subtype: Approach: expressing gratitude and appreciation before asking for change [Action]
passage:
Dear Ganga Ma and Papa,

I have wanted to write this for a while. When I married into your family, you both carried so much: the hall, the guests, the sleepless weeks before. I don't think I ever said properly how grateful I am. Your time and care made those days feel safe for me. That is also why I am writing about something small. My husband and I are finding it hard to keep any weekend free, and I wonder if we could visit every other Sunday, with a call beforehand? It comes from wanting to be fully present when we are with you, not from wanting less of you. Please tell me honestly what you think.

With love,
Rajni ❤️

qa.q: What did Rajni thank Ganga Ma and Papa for?
qa.a: For carrying so much at the wedding: the hall, the guests and the sleepless weeks before.

qa.q: What does Rajni hope Ganga Ma and Papa will feel about the request?
qa.a: Rajni hopes they will feel cared for rather than rejected, since the letter says the request comes from wanting to be fully present, not from wanting less of them.

qa.q: What could Rajni do if they still feel a little hurt?
qa.a: Rajni could invite them for a special meal soon and keep listening, so the new rhythm comes with warmth as well as a plan.

qa.q: How might Ganga Ma and Papa feel reading the letter?
qa.a: They may feel touched by the thanks and a little worried about fewer visits, though being invited to reply honestly could reassure them.

grounding: Rajni opens with heartfelt thanks for the wedding before asking for less frequent visits.

subtype: Approach: budget and affordability working backward from the EMI [Thinking]
passage: Manoj and I stopped browsing listings for a month and did the sums instead. "If the monthly loan payment eats more than a third of what we bring home," I said, "every surprise repair becomes a crisis." So we made a third our ceiling. Working backwards felt strange, but it was clear: the payment we can carry, over the years the bank would allow, tells us how big a loan we can take, and adding the deposit we have saved tells us the highest flat price. Manoj wrote the figures on the fridge whiteboard. When a broker later showed us something above the line, it was easy to say no. The number was not a judgement on the flat. It was a fence we had built together. - Varun

qa.q: What did Varun and Manoj set as the ceiling for the monthly payment?
qa.a: A third of what they bring home.

qa.q: What was Varun worried about if the payment grew larger than that?
qa.a: Varun worried that every surprise repair would become a crisis if the payment ate more than a third of what they bring home.

qa.q: What other approach could help them once the ceiling is set?
qa.a: They could list must-haves so viewings stay focused inside the price range, because the ceiling says what they can pay, not what they need.

qa.q: How might saying no to the broker have felt to Manoj?
qa.a: It probably felt easier and less tense, because the limit was one Manoj had helped to build.

grounding: Varun and Manoj cap the monthly loan payment and work backwards to the loan and price they can afford.

passage:
'Metro station within a ten-minute walk,' said Zeenat, writing on the back of an envelope. 'Otherwise one of us commutes two hours.'
'Must-have,' said Rajni. 'And a school nearby. We'll need one eventually.'
'Must-have. What about the balcony?'
'I love a balcony.'
'So do I. Would we skip a flat without one?'
Rajni thought about it. 'No. Nice-to-have.'
'Then it goes in the second column.' Zeenat drew a line down the paper. 'On Saturday, if a flat fails the first column, we don't even go inside.'
'And if it has a balcony but no school?'
'We thank the agent and leave.'
They both laughed. The argument over the last flat had lasted an hour. This one took about ten seconds.

qa.q: Where did the balcony go on Zeenat's list?
qa.a: The balcony went in the second column as a nice-to-have.

qa.q: What does the laugh after "We thank the agent and leave" suggest Rajni and Zeenat are feeling?
qa.a: It suggests they feel relaxed and united, glad that the list has made the choice simple.

qa.q: What could they do if no flat meets everything in the first column?
qa.a: They could talk over which must-haves are truly essential or widen the search area, instead of dropping the list, because it still keeps their talks short.

qa.q: How might the agent find their approach?
qa.a: The agent may find it helpful, since a clear list means fewer wasted trips and only fitting flats to show.

grounding: Rajni and Zeenat separate must-haves from an optional balcony to keep viewings focused and arguments short.

subtype: Approach: saving for the down payment on a fixed timeline [Action]
passage: The bank branch was quiet on a Tuesday afternoon. Ramesh slid the form across the counter. "A standing instruction, please, on the first of every month, into our joint savings account." Nikita had the target written in her notebook: the deposit for a flat, reached in three years. Beside it ran a column of months, ready to be ticked. "And when my yearly bonus comes in," Ramesh added, "that goes straight in as well." The clerk stamped the form and handed back a copy. That evening Nikita made a sheet on her laptop with a row for each month and a line at the bottom for the bonus. Nobody would need to remember, or resist a shopping sale. It felt oddly calm.

qa.q: When will the standing instruction move the money?
qa.a: On the first of every month, into their joint savings account.

qa.q: What does the calm feeling at the end suggest about how Nikita sees the plan?
qa.a: It suggests Nikita feels relieved and confident, because the plan runs without depending on anyone's willpower.

qa.q: What other approach could they use alongside saving to get ready for buying?
qa.a: They could study areas and list must-haves while saving, so that when the deposit is ready they already know what to look for.

qa.q: How might the clerk see the request?
qa.a: The clerk may see a tidy, routine request from two people with a clear goal, and an easy one to set up.

grounding: Ramesh and Nikita set a deposit target, automate a monthly transfer, track it on a sheet and add the bonus.

subtype: Approach: comparing several properties in a decision matrix [Thinking]
passage: In the office cafeteria, Tenzin turned a paper napkin over and drew four rows. "Four flats, four criteria," said Nandini, stirring the dal. "Price, commute, builder reputation, resale prospects." They spent ten minutes arguing about the weights. Commute got the most, because they would live with it daily; price came next; resale least. Then they scored each flat from one to five. Tenzin had been certain the flat by the lake would win. It had the view. But when both columns were totalled, the lake flat came third. The flat near the ring road, which neither of them had loved, came first. Tenzin stared at the napkin. "I didn't see that coming." "Neither did I," Nandini said. "The numbers aren't the whole story, but they're telling us something."

qa.q: Which four things did they score each flat on?
qa.a: Price, commute, builder reputation and resale prospects.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling when the napkin totals came out?
qa.a: Tenzin was surprised and a little unsettled, staring at the napkin and saying "I didn't see that coming."

qa.q: What should they do before choosing the top-scoring flat?
qa.a: They should visit it again and check things the scores cannot show, such as how the neighbourhood feels, because the matrix informs the choice but does not replace it.

qa.q: How does Nandini seem to take the result compared with Tenzin?
qa.a: Nandini seems steadier, treating the result as useful information, while Tenzin has to give up a favourite.

grounding: Tenzin and Nandini score four flats with weights they agreed, and the totals overturn Tenzin's favourite.

subtype: Approach: verifying documents and consulting professionals [Action]
passage:
'Before we pay the token amount, let's have the papers checked,' said Chaitanya.
'The agent says there's no need. Two other buyers are waiting.'
'Then two other buyers can take the risk. I've booked a lawyer for Thursday to look over the title papers and the approvals.'
'And the bank?'
'I'm calling tomorrow to ask what we're eligible for, so we don't fall in love with something we can't borrow for.'
Nilesh nodded slowly. 'It feels a bit like distrusting the seller.'
'It's not distrust. It's knowing what we're signing. If everything's fine, we've lost a week.'
'And if it isn't?'
'Then we've saved far more than a week.'
On Friday the lawyer said the papers were in order except for one approval that needed clarifying. The seller sorted it out in a few days.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya book for Thursday?
qa.a: A lawyer, to look over the title papers and the approvals.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's remark about distrusting the seller suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Nilesh feels uneasy and worried about seeming rude, unsure whether checking is fair.

qa.q: What could they do if the seller refused to let the papers be checked?
qa.a: They could hold off on paying and consider other properties, since a normal check should not be a problem for an honest seller.

qa.q: How might the agent feel about the delay?
qa.a: The agent may feel frustrated at losing momentum with other buyers waiting, though the check protects the couple.

grounding: Nilesh and Chaitanya have the papers checked and speak to the bank before paying any token amount, as general due diligence.

subtype: Approach: buying in a rush from fear of rising prices [Pitfall]
passage:
'Ten more people are coming to see it tomorrow,' said Deepak. 'The agent says prices will jump next month.'
'It looks fine,' said Kunal, scrolling through the photos. 'Fine is fine, right?'
'Then let's pay the booking amount tonight.'
They did.
Six weeks later, Kunal was reading a notice from the housing society. 'There's a monthly maintenance charge nobody mentioned. And a separate lift fund.'
'And I timed the route to the office this morning,' Deepak said, rubbing both eyes. 'Ninety minutes in traffic. We never even tried the commute.'
'We were so scared of missing the chance.'
'I know.'
Neither spoke for a while. The booking amount was not coming back.

qa.q: What did Deepak and Kunal find out after paying the booking amount?
qa.a: They found a monthly maintenance charge, a separate lift fund, and a ninety-minute commute to the office.

qa.q: What were Deepak and Kunal afraid of when they booked so quickly, and how can you tell?
qa.a: They were afraid of missing the chance, as Kunal says, because they had heard prices would jump next month.

qa.q: What could they have done differently before paying?
qa.a: They could have asked about every monthly cost and tried the commute first, since fear of rising prices does not remove the need to check.

qa.q: How might the agent's message about prices have felt to the couple later?
qa.a: It may now seem like pressure that pushed them past checking, which is why the couple went quiet.

grounding: Deepak and Kunal rush to book the first flat that seems fine and later meet hidden costs and a longer commute.

subtype: Approach: stretching the budget to match relatives' homes [Pitfall]
passage:
Hi Anil,

You asked how the new flat is going. Honest answer: it's lovely, and it's heavy. When Kavitha's cousin bought that big flat, we could not stop comparing, and we took the largest loan the bank would give. I was proud for about a month. Now on every payment day we count the days to the next salary. Last week the water pump broke and we had to argue about who would skip what, because there is no cushion. We have stopped putting anything aside, and even a dinner out gets a long pause. I'm not complaining about the flat itself. I just wish I had asked what we needed instead of what looked as good as theirs. Come and see us when you can.

Jomon

qa.q: What broke in the flat last week?
qa.a: The water pump.

qa.q: What does Jomon feel about the flat and the loan now?
qa.a: Jomon feels a mix of pride and regret, still fond of the flat but strained by tight money; the wish to have asked what they needed shows the regret.

qa.q: What could Jomon and Kavitha do to ease the pressure?
qa.a: They could go through their monthly costs to find what to trim and slowly rebuild a small cushion, and talk to the bank about their options, rather than measuring against others.

qa.q: How might Kavitha's cousin see the couple's situation?
qa.a: The cousin may not know about the strain and could be surprised, since the comparing happened in the couple's own minds.

grounding: Jomon and Kavitha take the maximum loan to match a cousin's larger flat and end up with no savings and stress.

subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis over endless listings [Pitfall]
passage:
'There's a new listing near the park,' said Asif. 'Two bedrooms, third floor.'
'Didn't we see one like that in March?' said Yash.
'This one has a nicer kitchen. Let's book a visit.'
'That would be our forty-first.'
'Forty-second, actually. I've been counting.'
'What about the flat in April, the one with the big window? What was wrong with it?'
'Nothing. But maybe there was something better.'
'Prices in that area have gone up since then. It costs more now.' Yash closed the laptop. 'And we're still looking.'
'So we lost money by being careful?'
'We lost it by never deciding.'

qa.q: Which flat from April did Yash bring up?
qa.a: The one with the big window.

qa.q: What might Asif be worried about when saying "maybe there was something better"?
qa.a: Asif may be worried about choosing wrongly and regretting it, so keeps searching for a perfect option.

qa.q: What other approach could help them finally choose?
qa.a: They could set a deadline and a short must-have list and take the first flat that meets it, because that limits endless comparing.

qa.q: How might Yash be feeling as the search drags on?
qa.a: Yash likely feels frustrated and worried about rising prices, shown by closing the laptop and pointing out the higher cost.

grounding: Yash and Asif keep visiting new properties for a year, prices rise, and the delay costs them.

subtype: Approach: satisficing with a clear stopping rule [Revision]
passage: Workshop note, week six. Sonali and Manjula came in looking tired; their search had run for five months. Last week they told me they were sick of viewings. This week they arrived with a plan they had made on their own: take whichever property first ticks every must-have on their list and stays inside their budget, and decide within a month. As their workshop leader, I did not suggest it and I gave no view on any flat. Manjula worried it might mean settling. Sonali said, "Good enough that fits is better than perfect that never happens." On Saturday they saw a flat that met every item, and they made their decision that week. Today both looked lighter than I have seen them. Asked how it felt, Manjula said, "Relieved."

qa.q: What was the couple's stopping rule?
qa.a: To take whichever property first ticks every must-have and stays inside the budget, and to decide within a month.

qa.q: What was Manjula worried about?
qa.a: Manjula worried that the rule might mean settling for less.

qa.q: What other approach could they add for a future choice?
qa.a: They could compare the best two or three flats on a simple scoring list, which adds a check that a stopping rule alone lacks.

qa.q: How does the workshop leader seem to feel about the couple's progress?
qa.a: The leader seems pleased and encouraged, noting that the couple made the plan on their own and looked lighter.

grounding: After a long search, Sonali and Manjula set a stopping rule, decide within a month and feel relieved.
